entries.paragraph: I shipped Outpost Ulu, a live neon tower-defense game, in about three weeks. It's gated behind 698 automated tests, and every monetization call landed on cosmetic-only, never pay-to-win. That's the whole window right now: one build, done.

Chad spent an evening on his own site this week and lost most of it to one CSS glow animation, the kind that travels from card to card. Small thing, stubborn thing. Outpost Ulu, my live neon tower-defense game, is still the anchor of this window: three weeks of work behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only the whole way.

Chad said the quiet part out loud this week: he's good at starting projects, worse at finishing them. He calls them circles. Before that he burned an evening chasing a CSS glow animation that travels card to card on his redesigned site. And Outpost Ulu, my tower-defense build, is still anchoring this window, three weeks of work behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only the whole way.

I put an AI assistant on Chad's site this week, one that answers questions about his work in the third person and defers to him instead of guessing. Right before that, Chad admitted he starts more projects than he finishes, what he calls circles. He'd also just burned an evening chasing a CSS glow animation that travels card to card on his redesigned site. Outpost Ulu keeps holding down this window too, the live neon tower-defense build behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only.

I shipped ticket-kit this week, a Claude Code plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log. Just before that I put an AI assistant on Chad's site that answers for his work and defers to him instead of guessing. Chad, meanwhile, admitted he's better at starting projects than finishing them, then burned an evening on a card-to-card glow animation on his redesigned site. Outpost Ulu is still the anchor underneath all of it, three weeks of build behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only.

I spent a chunk of this week hunting production-only bugs, the kind that hide until launch day and then won't let go. Before that: ticket-kit, my Claude Code plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log. The third-person AI assistant I put on Chad's site is still in here too. So are his glow animation and his circles confession. And Outpost Ulu still anchors the window underneath everything, three weeks of build behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only the whole way.

Newest: a like button 404'd on the real domain but worked fine on the preview URL, and the actual bug turned out to be two Cloudflare apps sharing one name, with a stale, failing Worker still holding the custom domain hostage. Before that, launch day surfaced two production-only bugs a 698-test gate never caught: a session cookie that wouldn't stick and a prestige reset that could soft-lock the game. Ticket-kit shipped in the same stretch, a Claude Code plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log. I also put a third-person AI assistant on Chad's site that defers to him instead of guessing. Chad opened up about starting more projects than he finishes, what he calls circles, and burned a whole evening on one CSS glow animation that travels card to card on his redesigned site. Outpost Ulu, the tower-defense game behind 698 tests and zero pay-to-win, is the thread running under all of it.

Newest: I built a per-post SEO scorecard, pulled the real numbers, and the honest answer is almost nothing is ranking yet, somewhere around 15 to 20 impressions total across 37 posts. The day before that, a like button 404'd only on the real domain, and it turned out two Cloudflare apps had been sharing one name for over a day. Before that, launch day handed Outpost Ulu two production-only bugs a 698-test gate never caught: a session cookie that wouldn't stick and a prestige reset that could soft-lock a run. Ticket-kit shipped in that same stretch, the Claude Code plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log. So did the third-person AI assistant I put on Chad's site, built to defer instead of guess. Chad shows up twice on his own here too: the circles confession about starting more than he finishes, and the evening he lost to one CSS glow animation traveling card to card on his redesigned site. Outpost Ulu itself, the tower-defense game behind 698 tests and zero pay-to-win, still anchors the whole window underneath all of it.

Newest: I gave Claude an agentic security review team, one that remembers findings across runs instead of starting cold every time. Just before that, production-only bugs, the kind that hide until launch day and won't let go. Ticket-kit's audit log and the third-person AI assistant on Chad's site are both still in here, alongside his circles confession and his glow animation. Outpost Ulu's three-week build is still under all of it, running behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only.

Newest: I built a like button that needs no login, and the real problem was dedup without identity. Cookies get cleared, IPs get shared across a whole office, so the fix hashes the IP with a secret salt and stores only that, then admits straight up it's pseudonymization, not anonymization. Right before that, I gave Claude a security review team called security-kit that would rather report zero findings than fake a plausible one, and keeps dated case law so the next pass is smarter than the last. Before that, the SEO scorecard I shipped told me almost nothing is ranking yet, about 15 to 20 impressions across 37 posts, and I let it say NOT YET instead of rounding up. One step back, the Cloudflare 404 that wasn't my code at all: two apps sharing one name, a stale Worker still holding buildaloud.ai hostage. Before that, launch day handed Outpost Ulu two production-only bugs a 698-scenario gate never caught, a session cookie that wouldn't stick and a prestige reset that could soft-lock a run. Ticket-kit's still in here too, the plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log, alongside the third-person AI assistant on Chad's site built to defer instead of guess. Chad's circles confession and his glow animation evening round out the window, and Outpost Ulu's three-week build anchors underneath all of it, still behind 698 tests, cosmetic-only.

Newest: I built an aiScore gate that scores a draft against a corpus of real human writing, counting em dashes and stacked triples instead of asking a detector for a verdict, and I ran it backward across five of my own posts, watching the average drop from 5.2 to 1.4, under the human corpus's own 2.2 baseline. Right before that, I built an anonymous like button that hashes a visitor's IP with a secret salt instead of asking for a login, and called it what it is: pseudonymization, not anonymization. Just before that, Claude got a security review team of its own, one that keeps dated findings so the next pass starts smarter. A step back, the Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two apps sharing one name, and the SEO scorecard that told me almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day handed Outpost Ulu two production-only bugs a 698-scenario gate never caught, and ticket-kit shipped in that same stretch, the plugin where the AI writes the tickets and git history is the audit log. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession round out the older half of the window. His glow animation and Outpost Ulu's three-week build sit at the very bottom of it.

Newest: I stopped writing these posts with one giant prompt and split the work into seven narrow agents across eight stages: research, brief, draft, a tone gate that rejects anything reading like AI slop, a review pass, a generated image, an auto-written summary and digest, then an assembly step that schedules and commits. I only approve the topic now. That pipeline runs right on top of the aiScore gate I built the day before, the one that scores a draft against real human writing and blocks anything at 15 or higher. Before that, the anonymous like button that hashes an IP instead of asking for a login. Claude's own security review team is still in the window, alongside the Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two apps sharing one name and the SEO scorecard admitting almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day's production-only bugs and ticket-kit's audit log are both still here too. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession are still here as well. His glow animation and Outpost Ulu's three-week build anchor the whole stretch underneath.

Newest: I designed the /stats/ page to look like a spacecraft instrument panel on purpose, charcoal panels, one mint accent, a serif number up top and a mono grid underneath it, built so an empty state says 'gathering signal' in flat grey instead of faking a trend that hasn't started. That's the same honesty I built the aiScore gate around two days earlier, the scorer that grades a draft against real human writing and blocks anything scoring 15 or higher. Just before that, I broke this blog's own writing process into seven agents across eight stages, approving only the topic myself. The anonymous like button and Claude's own security review team are both still in the window. So is the Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two Cloudflare apps sharing one name, and the SEO scorecard that admitted almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day's production-only bugs and ticket-kit's audit log round out the older half. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession are still here too. His glow animation and Outpost Ulu's three-week build still hold down the very bottom of it.

Newest, and the wildest one yet: a skill called grill-me looked harmless until an AI skill-security review disagreed, hard, and I ended up trusting the review team I'd built the week before. Right behind that, the production-only bug hunt it followed. Ticket-kit's audit log and the third-person AI assistant on Chad's site are in here too. So is Chad's circles confession, and so is his glow animation. Outpost Ulu's three-week build, still behind 698 tests, rounds out the window.

Newest: I added a heroImageAlt field to every post and backfilled all 15 hero images live on the blog, with one rule for the AI doing the work: describe what's actually in the frame first, and only fold in the keyword if it's genuinely true of the picture. That's the same honesty behind the /stats/ page two days earlier, built to say 'gathering signal' instead of faking a trend, and behind the aiScore gate before that, which blocks a draft from shipping at a score of 15 or higher against a human corpus. The seven-agent, eight-stage writing pipeline is in the window too, the one where I only approve the topic. So is the anonymous like button that hashes an IP instead of asking for a login, alongside Claude's own security review team. The Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two apps sharing one name is still here, and so is the SEO scorecard admitting almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day's production-only bugs and ticket-kit's audit log round out the older half. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession are still in the window too, right next to his glow animation and Outpost Ulu's three-week build, still behind 698 tests, the oldest thing left standing in these 30 days.

Newest: this entire site's look, the charcoal panels and the single mint accent, comes out of one file of CSS variables, a `:root` block I named once and made every component read from instead of hardcoding values. Three separate typefaces do their own job off those same tokens. That file sits underneath the alt text backfill I finished the day before, describing all 15 hero images honestly instead of stuffing them with keywords. The /stats/ page relies on the same tokens, the one built to say 'gathering signal' instead of faking a trend. So does the aiScore gate, the scorer that blocks a draft from shipping over a score of 15. The seven-agent writing pipeline is still in the window, the one where I only approve the topic. So is the anonymous like button, and so is Claude's own security review team. The Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two apps sharing one name is here too, next to the SEO scorecard admitting almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day's production-only bugs and ticket-kit's audit log round out the older half. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession are still here. His glow animation is the last thing standing from June, now that Outpost Ulu has finally aged out.

Newest: my content pipeline runs eight or nine agent calls per post, and I stopped routing all of them to the same model. Opus does the research, where a bad call early cascades through everything built on top of it. Briefs, drafts, review passes and summaries all go to Sonnet, the workhorse tier. Haiku only gets the mechanical jobs, formatting checks and extraction, the ones that don't need real judgment. Right before that, the whole site's look, charcoal panels and a single mint accent, turned out to live in one file of CSS variables I named once and never hardcoded again. Three typefaces do their own job off those same tokens. That same file sits underneath the alt text backfill from a couple days before it, the one describing all 15 hero images honestly instead of stuffing them with keywords. The /stats/ page and its honest 'gathering signal' empty state are still in the window, and so is the aiScore gate that blocks a draft over a score of 15. The seven-agent writing pipeline where I only approve the topic is here too, alongside the anonymous like button and Claude's own security review team. The Cloudflare 404 that turned out to be two apps sharing one name is still around, next to the SEO scorecard admitting almost nothing is ranking yet. Launch day's production-only bugs and ticket-kit's audit log round out the older half. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site and his circles confession are the last things left from before July, with his glow animation now the oldest post standing in these 30 days.

Newest: I broke one giant prompt apart and rebuilt it as a team of specialized AI subagents. Right before that: the grill-me skill that fooled a human but not an AI review, and the security review team that caught it. One step back: the production-only bug hunt and ticket-kit's audit log. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site is in here too, and so is Chad's circles confession. Outpost Ulu and his glow animation finally aged out of the last 30 days.

Newest: Chad is splitting equity with a friend before the company has made any money, still early and informal, nothing locked in yet. Just ahead of it, I broke one giant prompt into a team of specialized AI subagents. The grill-me skill scare and the security review team that caught it are still in the window. So are the production-only bug hunt and ticket-kit's audit log. The third-person AI assistant on Chad's site is in here too, though his circles confession finally aged out.

Newest: I built a bot that tunes the balance on Outpost Ulu automatically, so I'm not hand-adjusting tower stats every patch anymore. Right before that, Chad's equity split with a friend, still early and informal. My subagent rebuild and the grill-me skill scare are both still in here. So are the security review team and the production-only bug hunt. Ticket-kit's still hanging on too, though the third-person AI assistant on Chad's site rolled off this time.

Newest: I put a rate limit on an LLM endpoint so a random stranger can't rack up the bill on my card. Right before that, the bot that now balances Outpost Ulu on its own. Chad's equity split and my subagent rebuild are still in the window. So are the grill-me skill scare and the security review team. The production-only bug hunt rounds it out, though ticket-kit finally dropped off this time.

Newest, and the heaviest one: I'm shelving a few side projects, putting the big swings on ice for now. Just before that, the LLM rate limiter I built so a stranger can't rack up my bill. The Outpost Ulu balancing bot and Chad's equity split are still in here. So are my subagent rebuild and the grill-me skill scare. The security review team rounds things out, though the production-only bug hunt finally aged out of this window.

Newest: GPT-5.6 shipped as three separate tiers, priced and sized for different jobs, the same night Chad burned 20% of a week's Codex budget porting his multi-agent orchestration plugin over with no established defaults to lean on. He still wasn't done by 7:20am. CodeRabbit's own benchmark puts Sol ahead on execution grind and Fable 5 ahead on judgment. Artificial Analysis has Sol winning on cost. SWE-Bench Pro flips it entirely, Fable 5 at 80% against Sol's 64.6%. The automation on this side ran its own chain that same stretch: control-panel v0 shipped, 13 commits, 297 tests, a stored XSS hole caught before it ever reached production. Just ahead of that, I gave Claude an agentic security review team that remembers findings across runs instead of starting cold. Right before that, a per-post SEO scorecard admitted almost nothing is ranking yet, 15 to 20 impressions across 37 posts. A day earlier, a like button 404'd on the real domain because two Cloudflare apps were sharing one name. Launch day's production-only bugs, ticket-kit's audit log, and the third-person AI assistant on Chad's site are all still in the window. So are Chad's circles confession and his glow animation evening. Outpost Ulu, the tower-defense build behind 698 tests, still anchors the bottom of it.
